analysis.one_liner: Requires private insurance plans to cover three primary care and three mental health visits at no out-of-pocket cost.
analysis.headline: H.R. 3550 died in committee with no vote: it was referred to three House committees and its health subcommittee in May 2021 and never advanced before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal law so that group health plans and private insurers must pay the full cost of the first three primary care visits and three behavioral health (mental health) visits each year, with no copays, deductibles, or other cost sharing. It also barred insurers from setting extra treatment limits or lower reimbursement rates just for those six visits. The bill was introduced by Rep. Lauren Underwood and referred to three House committees, where it stayed until Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private or employer health insurance who skip checkups or mental health care because of copays and deductibles. The visits would be free the moment they walk in, and people could see primary care doctors, therapists, social workers, counselors, psychologists, and other qualified providers. Studies cited in favor of similar bills show cost is a leading reason people skip care, so removing it for a handful of visits would catch problems earlier, including mental health conditions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured people skipping care over copays

how_it_helps.text: Group health plans and health insurance issuers must cover three primary care visits and three behavioral health care visits per plan year with no cost sharing of any kind.

Insurers may not apply treatment limits to those visits that are more restrictive than limits on other covered visits, and must reimburse them at the same rate as other primary and behavioral health visits, preventing insurers from undermining the requirement with fine print.

The bill covers a wide range of behavioral health providers, including psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, mental health counselors, and marriage and family therapists, so the free visits can actually be used for therapy and treatment, not just a brief screening.
The bill also amends the high-deductible health plan rules so those visits count as permitted preventive care without a deductible, removing a tax-law barrier for people on high-deductible plans.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance companies and the employers and consumers who fund premiums. Plans would absorb the cost of the free visits, and insurers and employer plans would likely pass some of that cost through in premiums; the bill sets no funding source, so the cost stays in the private system.

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises insurers' costs, and insurers and employers would likely pass some of it to everyone through higher premiums, so people who never use the visits would pay a little more.

Three visits per year is a small floor; after the three free visits, regular copays and deductibles apply, so the bill helps people take a first step but does not make ongoing therapy or treatment affordable.
Free care for six visits is not free overall — it is shifted into premiums — and the requirement applies to plans beginning two years after enactment, so help would have been slow to arrive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: six no-cost visits a year lowers the barrier to a first checkup or a first therapy appointment, which is where untreated problems are often caught. The cost is a small premium increase spread across everyone with private insurance. The bigger weakness is design: three visits will not carry someone through a course of mental health treatment, and the bill leaves the rest of cost sharing untouched. Even so, for people who skip care because of the price at the front desk, this would have helped.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee the next day, and no committee ever acted on it before Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Lauren Underwood introduced the bill on May 25, 2021, joined by Reps. Schrier and Porter.
The same day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means Committees, and the next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
It had 7 Democratic cosponsors, no Republicans, and no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote appears in its action history before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The CRS summary confirms the bill's single requirement: coverage of three primary care and three behavioral health visits per plan year without cost sharing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors, who never had to absorb the cost of the no-cost visits, and no one else. People who skip care over copays gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, who avoided the mandate

sides.party_line_note: All eight supporters (sponsor plus 7 cosponsors) were House Democrats and no Republicans signed on; no recorded opposition action appears in the record, and the bill simply never left committee.

industries.note: They would have to pay for six no-cost visits per member per year and forgo copays and deductibles on them, and would likely shift the cost into premiums. The bill also barred them from using restrictive limits or lower rates on those visits. The mandate never took effect because the bill died in committee.
Free visits would send more patients to therapists, counselors, psychologists, and social workers who are named as qualified providers in the bill, paid at the plan's normal rates.
The bill requires reimbursement equal to that of other covered visits, so practices would see more patients at normal rates rather than absorbing free visits.
As plan sponsors under ERISA and the tax code they would bear part of the added benefit cost, but healthier workers who catch problems early can mean lower costs over time.
